summary: C: The avatar keeps re-litigating the decision to recruit a bandit at all, out loud, in front of Jost, apparently unaware or unbothered that he's standing right there for it. Jost, unbothered in turn, just waits for them to finish. B: The avatar admits the re-litigating isn't really about Jost -- it's the habit, they do it to every call whether it worked out or not. Jost points out that's exhausting to watch and probably worse to live inside, and offers the one thing his own approach has going for it: once a thing's decided, sleeping through the rest of the argument is free. A: The avatar admits they've never once managed to just let a decision be decided; Jost admits his own version of that isn't peace, it's refusing to spend anything on a question after the fact because spending on it before never worked either. Neither talks the other into changing. The avatar starts running fewer post-mortems out loud where Jost has to hear them; Jost starts actually staying awake for the ones that are about him.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich). Scorpion's failure mode ('carries it long after it stopped being useful') set directly against Ram's virtue (decisive, doesn't look back) -- two opposite relationships to a decision once it's made. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar reviews Ricberta's levy reports and flags the handwriting as suspiciously clean for a dictated report; Ricberta deflects, badly, in a way that would fool someone with less reason to notice competence being hidden. B: The avatar doesn't push it in front of the levy, which Ricberta clocks as deliberate -- an administrator who argues everything in the open chose not to, this once. She starts wondering what else the avatar's decided not to argue about, out loud, for someone's sake. A: The avatar admits they know exactly why she's hiding it -- rank protects nothing once someone above you decides your competence is a liability, and they've watched it happen to smarter people than either of them. Ricberta, who's spent years managing the secret alone, gets the first offer of institutional cover from someone with the rank to actually make it stick: the avatar will vouch for her literacy being an asset, not a flag, whenever she decides to stop hiding it. She doesn't take the offer. She does, for the first time, believe someone meant it.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun). Direct tie: Ricberta's own note ('secretly literate... literacy is a deputy tiebreak') is exactly the kind of hidden-competence-as-liability the avatar's own institutional position lets them actually shield, unlike the peers who could only ever gossip about it. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar keeps re-pushing an already-overruled requisition for more winter-dole grain. Maren, who runs the dole line, has heard every version of this argument already, from people with more rank and less follow-through. B: Maren notices the avatar doesn't stop arguing once the requisition is denied a second time -- goes over the ledgers alone, at night, still building a case nobody asked to hear again. She starts leaving the real capacity numbers where they will find them. A: The avatar admits the arguing was never strategy -- walking away from a wrong call feels like the actual failure, rank or no rank. Maren, who has watched people put on a Warden's mask specifically so they can keep making that same call without it costing them anything, tells them plainly: don't go numb to it, get useful instead -- and hands over the dole line's real numbers, unfiltered. S (romance): the avatar stops arguing to be right and starts arguing with Maren's numbers instead of past them; Maren, who pours herself out for a whole line of strangers every winter, finds the one person she doesn't have to ration the truth for.
notes: Avatar=Scorpion is new, off the avatar's own note ('level 1 administrator... voiced and argumentative'), read as someone who keeps re-raising a decision everyone else has let rank settle, which is the Scorpion's virtue ('carries the grudge that keeps everyone honest') read institutionally rather than personally. Maren=Crab is new, off her own note ('winter-dole healer' -- loyalty to the people in her line over the crown's actual allotment, the Crab's own failure mode read as triage under scarcity) -- a deliberate second Crab, distinct from Ricberta's (military/secrecy) by being medical/scarcity-driven instead. Assembly-route avatar option per the original skeleton note; the avatar's sign is treated as fixed across both avatar chains in this pass, the same convention already used for an established unit's sign (Kest, Rinsa), not reassigned per pairing.

summary: C: The avatar asks Dietmar, bluntly, whether the gate-holding deed is a real strategic priority or a favor to an old soldier's ego. Dietmar, who has spent the obsolescence arc waiting for exactly this question and dreading it, doesn't dodge -- he just doesn't answer it either. B: The avatar keeps pushing, the way they push everything, and Dietmar finally admits he doesn't know the honest answer himself, which unsettles him more than the accusation would have. The avatar, who has never once let an unresolved question sit, recognizes something familiar in a man who's been avoiding his own for longer than the avatar's been alive. A: Dietmar admits the deed matters to him whether or not it's the correct use of the diadem's resources, and that not knowing which is the actual failure of the obsolescence, not the fading itself. The avatar, whose whole method is arguing until something resolves, doesn't resolve it for him -- just tells him some questions are worth keeping open on purpose, since a man who stops asking whether he still matters is worse off than one who keeps asking and doesn't like the answer yet. Dietmar takes the deed anyway. He stops needing it to be the right call to be worth doing.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Avatar=Scorpion from Avatar/Maren, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald). Scorpion's virtue ('carries the grudge that keeps everyone honest') applied to an institutional question rather than a personal one, directly confronting Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully'). Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The avatar wants Rinsa's account of the descent formally, for the record, the way they want everything -- structured, arguable, citable. Rinsa gives them the same answer she gives everyone: the descent isn't the kind of thing that survives being made into an argument. B: The avatar, who has never once accepted 'some things don't reduce to a case' as a real answer, keeps pressing, and Rinsa finally asks them plainly what they're actually trying to settle. The avatar admits it's the Venerated question -- they need it to be decidable, because the whole administration they're running depends on eventually deciding it. A: Rinsa tells them the descent doesn't decide anything either, it just goes down and comes back, same as it always has, for anyone -- the deciding was never hers to do, only the witnessing. The avatar, whose entire method is deciding things, has to sit with a source who refuses to resolve into a verdict on command. It doesn't change the avatar's strategy. It does change how they ask the next question, and the one after that -- less like a case to close, more like a person they're actually listening to.
notes: Avatar=Scorpion reused from Avatar/Maren. Rinsa's own already-stated sign, the Vessel, reused verbatim. Direct tie to the endgame: Rinsa's own note calls her 'the only unit who has BEEN down there' regarding whether the Venerated is dead, and the avatar's own note ('voiced and argumentative') makes them exactly the kind of person who'd try to litigate that fact instead of just receiving it. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Kest cases the avatar's own field desk out of habit before she's decided whether to join at all. The avatar catches her at it and, instead of reporting it, asks what she'd have taken. B: The avatar keeps re-litigating a call from chapters back -- a defection let stand, a resource not seized -- out loud, to no one in particular. Kest recognizes the arguing-with-someone-not-there rhythm immediately and says nothing, which is its own kind of recognition. A: Pressed, the avatar admits the second-guessing isn't doubt about the decision, it's refusing to let a bad outcome go unexamined just because it's over. Kest, still withholding her own reason for the same habit, offers only that she used to think the arguing meant something was wrong with her. The avatar's answer -- that it just means the argument mattered enough to keep -- is the first thing anyone's said about it that isn't trying to fix her. S (romance): the avatar's grudge against its own decisions and Kest's grudge against her own survival stop being separate arguments -- two people who never let a thing go finally aim it at the same target instead of at themselves.
notes: Kest's sign (the Twins) is her own already-stated sign, reused verbatim, not reassigned -- same treatment as in the Rinsa/Kest chain. Avatar=Scorpion reused from the Avatar/Maren chain above (see that chain's note for the grounding). Diadem-route avatar option per the original skeleton note.

summary: C: Ricberta doesn't trust the ford bandit the diadem just recruited, says so to his face, and expects him to either sulk or lie about it. Jost does neither -- agrees with her, cheerfully, and goes back to sleep. B: Jost keeps proving decisive exactly when the levy needs it and useless every other moment, which Ricberta, who's spent her whole career being the useful one nobody notices, finds harder to forgive than if he were simply bad at the job. A: Ricberta admits what actually bothers her -- Jost gets to be exactly what he is, unpolished and unbothered, while she's spent years managing a secret just to keep her post. Jost's answer surprises her: he tells her the sleeping is the only unpolished thing about him left, the rest -- the timing, the read on a fight -- he built on purpose, the same as she built her reading in secret; it just doesn't look like work from the outside. Ricberta stops mistaking his ease for laziness, and starts running her levy's ambush drills past him first.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun). Both diadem-route, ch_d02/ch_d03 -- a freshly-recruited ex-bandit and the levy sergeant who has every institutional reason to distrust him. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Emmerich's requisition ledgers keep coming up short after Jost's unit passes through. Jost's defense: he only takes what the count had already lost, not what's tracked -- which Emmerich hears as a personal insult to his ledger's accuracy. B: Jost, constitutionally unable to sit through Emmerich's line-by-line reconciliation meetings, starts falling asleep in them -- except Emmerich notices he only sleeps through the parts that don't matter, and stays sharp the instant a real number comes up. A: Emmerich admits the tidy showcase reports are half theater -- the Baron needs the diadem line to look competent more than he needs it accurate, and Emmerich is the one stuck producing both at once, terrified of the day the gap shows. Jost's answer isn't reassurance, it's a second set of eyes: he starts double-checking Emmerich's counts himself, badly, at a bandit's honest pace, so someone besides Emmerich is watching the real number. S (romance): Jost stops treating the ledger as a thing to raid and starts treating it as Emmerich's, specifically; Emmerich stops needing the Baron's audience once Jost's sloppy, loyal recount is the one he actually trusts.
notes: Jost=Ram is new, off his own note ('ford bandit; lucky sleeper' -- decisive the instant an ambush needs him, constitutionally unable to sit still for anything that isn't one -- the Ram's virtue/failure pair exactly). Emmerich=Lion is new, off his own note ('requisitions clerk; Baron showcase' -- a subordinate whose composure depends on being visibly valued by a superior; the Lion's failure mode, 'cannot take a demotion gracefully,' would hit him hardest of anyone on the roster). Both diadem-route (ch_d02/ch_d03), consistent with the original skeleton note.

summary: C: Tancred, fresh into the Pardoner line and taking absolution seriously, corners Jost about whether he regrets the banditry. Jost's honest answer -- not really, it kept him fed -- is not the answer Tancred was hoping to practice forgiving. B: Jost, watching Tancred grind through the Pardoner line's unglamorous requirements with real effort, admits he doesn't understand doing hard, boring work for a payoff that's mostly spiritual. Tancred doesn't try to convert him; he just keeps climbing, visibly, in front of Jost, which needles Jost more than a sermon would have. A: Jost admits the sleeping was never really laziness -- it's that trying and failing at something that mattered once cost him more than he could afford to keep paying, so he stopped trying at anything he couldn't walk away from clean. Tancred, who measures people by what they build rather than what they've survived, tells him the climbing doesn't have to be for something -- his own is mostly just proof he's still capable of it. Jost doesn't take up the climb. He does start showing up to watch, which is its own kind of practice.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm). Both diadem-route village-adjacent recruits (ch_d03), opposite relationships to their own pasts -- Jost's own note ('lucky sleeper') read as someone who stopped trying at anything he couldn't walk away from clean, set against Tancred's own note ('Pardoner line') as someone who took up trying, deliberately, as its own discipline. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Jost, newly diadem, meets Brandt on a joint assembly-diadem detail and clocks him immediately as the kind of soldier who'd have made his old ford ambushes a lot harder. Brandt, unbothered by being sized up by a reformed bandit, agrees, and asks if that's a compliment or a complaint. B: Jost admits it's a compliment, mostly -- he respects competence he can't get around, more than he respects competence he can. Brandt, who's used to being underestimated rather than flattered, doesn't quite know what to do with being professionally admired by a man who used to rob people for a living. A: Jost explains the respect plainly: Brandt's the kind of obstacle that would have made him actually plan instead of just getting lucky and sleeping through the rest, and Jost's spent his whole life avoiding exactly that kind of pressure. Brandt tells him that's not nothing -- most people never find out what they'd be if the easy way stopped working, and Jost's at least honest enough to know he never found out either. It's not quite a friendship. It's two men being plainly useful to each other's self-assessment, which for both of them is rarer than friendship.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Jost, half-asleep as usual, asks Solveig what it's like to already know how a flight's going to go before you take off. Solveig, prickly about the prophecy, tells him it isn't like that at all -- then admits she's never actually been asked the honest version of that question before. B: Solveig watches Jost sleep through the parts of a briefing that don't matter and snap awake the instant something does, and asks how he decides which is which without ever seeming to decide anything. Jost's answer -- he doesn't decide, it just arrives -- sounds uncomfortably close to her own family's account of the prophecy, except his always seems to serve him and hers never asks what she wants. A: Jost admits the sleeping isn't really about instinct, it's that deciding things in advance never worked out for him, so he stopped bothering and let the moment do the deciding instead -- which is either wisdom or the same trap her family's in, and he's honestly not sure which. Solveig, who has spent her whole life being handed an answer she didn't get to earn, tells him that not-deciding is a kind of freedom she's never once had, prophecy or no prophecy -- and asks him, seriously this time, to teach her how he does it, on purpose, instead of by accident.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Jost=Ram from Jost/Emmerich, Solveig=Vessel from Brandt/Solveig). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Ram's virtue read as decisiveness-without-premeditation, set directly against Vessel's failure mode ('belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody') -- inherited certainty vs earned spontaneity. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: They meet over dispatch schedules -- Sigrun keeps delivering orders faster than Ricberta's levies can act on them, and Ricberta's clipped complaints about 'impossible timing' are the whole conversation, on the surface a logistics gripe. B: Sigrun notices what nobody else on the levy roster does -- Ricberta reads the requisition slips before anyone reads them to her, a beat too fast for someone who's supposed to need them read aloud. She doesn't say it in front of the others, which is its own kind of answer. A: Ricberta admits it outright, expecting the usual calculus (a literate sergeant is a sergeant someone above her will want moved, watched, or replaced). Sigrun's response isn't reassurance, it's redirection -- she starts routing dispatches so Ricberta's own reading gets used instead of hidden, folding the secret into the job instead of asking Ricberta to keep choosing between them. S (romance): what holds is exactly what the signs promised and neither one flinched from -- Sigrun says the true thing at the worst moment, and the worst moment turns out to be the only time Ricberta would have believed her. Loyalty that used to end at 'the people already inside the wall' widens by exactly one.
notes: Signs assigned per the signs tab's own methodology (argued from behaviour, not a keyword): Ricberta=Crab off her own note ('secretly literate... literacy is a deputy tiebreak' -- guards a secret to protect her position and the people under her, the Crab's own failure mode -- loyalty to people over the cause -- is the exact shape of hiding competence to keep her sergeant's post rather than risk promotion scrutiny). Sigrun=Archer off hers ('courier rider' -- ranges out, returns with news, the Archer's failure mode 'says the true thing at the worst moment' is the literal action that breaks the support open in the B->A transition).

summary: C: A diadem sergeant and an assembly sergeant compare levies the way any two career soldiers on opposite sides of a fence do -- whose men hold better, whose gate matters more. B: Ricberta needles Brandt about the assembly's discipline; Brandt, who has never once needed to be smarter than his post to keep it, doesn't have a clever answer and says so, plainly, which throws Ricberta more than an argument would have. A: Ricberta admits the real grievance was never about discipline -- it's that being smart enough to need to hide it made her career something to manage rather than something to just do, and Brandt's uncomplicated competence looks like a life she didn't get offered. Brandt, who has spent his own career being underestimated as simple, tells her that holding a gate without needing anyone to notice you're clever at it is its own kind of hard -- and that he'd take her levy's discipline over his own gate crew's, if either of them ever needed to say so out loud, which sergeants generally don't.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun, Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig). Cross-route mirror-professionals (both sergeants, both lance/armor), post-convergence. Platonic chain, capped at A -- explicitly not folded into either unit's existing romance chain (Ricberta/Sigrun, Brandt/Solveig).

summary: C: Solveig's courier route clips past Ricberta's levy on a fixed schedule; Ricberta, protective of her men's drill time, complains that the flyovers spook the recruits. Solveig, used to complaints about the prophecy, is almost relieved this one's just about noise. B: Ricberta admits, once the actual complaint's addressed, that the flyovers aren't really the problem -- it's that Solveig gets to be visibly exceptional at her job in a way Ricberta's spent years making sure she never looks like. Solveig, who's never once gotten to choose how visible her own competence is, doesn't know what to do with someone envying the choice she never had. A: Solveig admits the visibility isn't a choice, it's inheritance -- the family's prophecy makes sure everyone's always watching, whether she's earned it that day or not. Ricberta, whose whole discipline is deciding exactly how much competence gets shown, tells her that's the one thing she'd never trade her hiding for: at least the hiding is hers to manage. Neither envies the other by the end. They do start comparing notes on managing an audience neither one asked for.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun, Solveig=Vessel from Brandt/Solveig). Crab's failure mode (competence deliberately hidden) set against Vessel's failure mode ('belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody') -- two different relationships to being watched, neither one chosen. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Ricberta's levy reports keep tripping over the same manifest discrepancies Emmerich's already flagged; she corners Kheldar herself, expecting a smuggler to be easier to intimidate than a clerk. B: Kheldar isn't intimidated, but he is curious -- a sergeant hiding her own literacy has more in common with a man who hides his own trail than either would admit outright, and he says so. Ricberta doesn't confirm it, which he takes, correctly, as confirmation. A: Ricberta admits the parallel's fair and she hates it -- hiding competence and hiding a trail aren't the same crime, but they're the same posture, always calculating what gets seen. Kheldar, who has never once been caught out by someone reading his own tells back at him, offers her something closer to respect than a threat: he'll route his discrepancies around her levy specifically, professional courtesy, one hider of things to another. Ricberta doesn't thank him. She does stop reporting the ones that don't cost her men anything.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun, Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest). Crab's failure mode (competence hidden to protect a position) recognized by Scorpion's own trade (a man built around not being pinned down) as the same posture from two different professions. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Ricberta, sizing up the assembly's last old-order knight the way she sizes up every soldier who might outrank her competence, asks Torvald plainly why he still takes orders from officers half his age. Torvald's answer is short: someone has to hold the post, rank was never the point. B: Ricberta needles at that -- rank is always the point, she's built a whole second life managing exactly how much competence she can afford to show without it costing her the post -- and Torvald, who has never once had to hide anything about what he's capable of, doesn't understand the calculation until she spells it out. A: Torvald admits her calculation is the harder discipline -- his own loyalty cost him grief, not strategy, because there was never anyone left to manage the appearance for. Ricberta hears, for the first time, an answer to 'what happens once the hiding isn't necessary anymore' that isn't a threat: it's just a man who outlived the need for it, and still chose to keep serving anyway. She doesn't stop hiding. She starts believing there's a version of not having to.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Ricberta=Crab from Ricberta/Sigrun, Torvald=Crab from Dietmar/Torvald). Deliberately paired as a second Crab mirror (after Solveig/Rinsa's Vessel mirror) -- argued as distinct temporal positions on the same failure mode: Ricberta's loyalty protects a future inside a system that still exists, Torvald's preserves a past system that's already gone. Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Emmerich's requisition reports keep crediting Waldrada's flights with cargo she never actually delivered -- an accounting shortcut, not malice -- and she calls him on it in front of the Baron, which he does not forgive quickly. B: Waldrada, still weighing whether the diadem's own bookkeeping is any more honest than the assembly's she defected from, starts actually reading Emmerich's ledgers instead of just resenting them, and finds he flags his own errors before anyone else catches them -- more than was ever asked of her under the assembly. A: Emmerich admits the showcase reports are half theater -- the Baron needs the diadem line to look competent more than he needs it accurate, and Emmerich is stuck producing both truths at once. Waldrada recognizes the position exactly: performing loyalty while the real math tells a different story. S (romance): Waldrada stops weighing whether the diadem deserves any more trust than the assembly did; Emmerich gets one ledger he doesn't have to cook -- hers, kept scrupulously, on his side, for reasons that have nothing to do with the Baron.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains above (Emmerich=Lion from Jost/Emmerich, Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda) -- same unit, same sign, not reassigned per pairing, the same convention as Kest/Rinsa's fixed unit signs. Both diadem-route (ch_d02), consistent with the original skeleton note -- a different-sex option distinct from Waldrada's cross-route pairing with Edda above.

summary: C: Emmerich, terrified of being caught in an error in front of the Baron, asks Anselm -- half-joking -- whether the order has a blessing for accountants. Anselm's answer is a real one: no, because accuracy isn't a virtue their doctrine tracks, only intent, which Emmerich finds both useless and strangely comforting. B: Emmerich admits the fear isn't really about the Baron, it's that being visibly valued is the only thing keeping him from being reassigned somewhere he can't fix anything at all. Anselm, whose entire crisis is that he understands too many sides of a question to condemn or bless cleanly, recognizes a kindred fear dressed up as competence anxiety instead of doubt. A: Anselm offers him the one piece of his dissolved theology that still holds together: intent survives an error even when the ledger doesn't, and a Baron who can't tell the difference was never the audience worth keeping anyway. Emmerich doesn't stop being anxious about the showcase. He does start keeping a second, private ledger -- the honest one -- and tells Anselm it's the closest thing he has to a confession, unprompted, which is more than the monk's actual congregation has managed lately.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Emmerich=Lion from Jost/Emmerich, Anselm=Fishes from Tancred/Anselm). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence, same convention as Waldrada/Edda and Dietmar/Torvald. Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully') read as showcase-anxiety, met by Fishes' virtue (understands too many sides to condemn cleanly) offering the one piece of doctrine that actually helps. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Emmerich's ledgers have a Kheldar-shaped hole in them that he's known about for months and never reported, which eats at him more than any error he's actually caught. B: Kheldar, amused, points out that reporting him would cost Emmerich the one manifest that always balances -- a smuggler who's good enough to make the books look clean is worth more to a showcase clerk than an honest one who isn't. Emmerich hates that this is true and hates more that he'd already worked it out himself. A: Emmerich admits the real fear isn't Kheldar, it's that the Baron's showcase was never really about accuracy, and Kheldar's the only person who's said so to his face instead of letting him find out alone. Kheldar, who has made a career out of being the discrepancy no one can afford to close, offers him something closer to honesty than either expected: he'll keep the numbers clean exactly as long as it's useful to both of them, no further promises -- which is more truth than the Baron's ever gotten out of either man.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Emmerich=Lion from Jost/Emmerich, Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest above). Direct mechanical tie: Emmerich's own note ('requisitions clerk') is exactly the job that should catch Kheldar's own note ('manifest discrepancy thread') -- the chain is built on the clerk quietly choosing not to catch him. Platonic/rivalry chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Emmerich's showcase reports keep quietly using Dietmar's gate-holding deed as proof the diadem's old guard still delivers; Dietmar, who hasn't seen the actual language, is furious to learn he's being cited without being asked. B: Emmerich admits he needed a legend more than he needed permission -- the Baron wanted proof the diadem's past still justifies its present, and Dietmar's deed was the only material he had. Dietmar, whose entire crisis is needing to still be seen as relevant, discovers being used for exactly that purpose feels worse than being ignored would have. A: Dietmar admits what's actually under the fury: being cited as a legend and being seen as a person aren't the same thing, and Emmerich's showcase does the first while doing nothing for the second. Emmerich, whose own fear is being reduced to a number in someone else's report, recognizes the complaint as his own, aimed back at him for once. He starts asking Dietmar what to actually write, instead of writing what's convenient and citing him after. Two men who each need to be seen accurately, not just seen, finally being that for each other instead of the Baron.
notes: Both units already carry the Lion sign from their own established chains (Emmerich from Jost/Emmerich, Dietmar from Dietmar/Torvald) -- a third sign-mirror pairing (after the Crab and Vessel mirrors), deliberately leaned into: two men whose shared failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully') collide directly when one uses the other as material instead of treating him as a person. Both diadem-route. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Emmerich's requisition math keeps assuming Torvald's unit needs resupply at the same rate as everyone else's; Torvald corrects him -- there's almost no unit left to supply, and the numbers should say so plainly instead of politely rounding up. B: Emmerich admits the rounding is deliberate -- an accurate line for 'one aging knight and no order behind him' would draw exactly the kind of attention that gets a unit quietly retired, and he's been protecting Torvald's post without asking. Torvald, who has never once let anyone manage his situation for him, is more unsettled by the kindness than he'd be by the threat. A: Torvald tells him plainly he'd rather be an accurate line than a flattered one -- being seen honestly and cut is still being seen, and Emmerich's whole fear is the opposite of that, being erased quietly instead of honestly. Emmerich, whose entire anxiety runs on being visibly valued, starts entering Torvald's numbers straight, no rounding, and finds the Baron never even notices. Neither of their fears turn out to be about the ledger at all.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Emmerich=Lion from Jost/Emmerich, Torvald=Crab from Ricberta/Torvald above). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Direct mechanical tie: Emmerich's own note ('requisitions clerk') applied literally to Torvald's own note ('last of a plague-gutted order') -- what an honest requisition line for a unit of one actually looks like. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Emmerich's ledgers have a Kest-shaped gap in them too, smaller than Kheldar's, sloppier, obviously amateur; he corners her about it mostly out of professional irritation at the imprecision. B: Kest, mid-argument with herself about whether admitting anything to a diadem clerk is smart, ends up telling him the truth almost by accident: she only takes what the count's already lost, same as always, and the imprecision he's annoyed by is just her not caring enough about his ledger to be careful. Emmerich, who cares about almost nothing as much as he cares about his ledger, finds this stranger than a real thief would be. A: Emmerich admits what's actually bothering him isn't the theft, it's being so easy to steal from without her even trying -- it means the showcase he's terrified of losing was never that impressive to begin with. Kest, whose whole method is arguing both sides until one wins, surprises herself by taking his side: she tells him the ledger's fine, she's just very good, and offers -- unprompted, a first for her -- to flag the actual gaps he should worry about instead. Emmerich gets a better auditor than he had. Kest gets the strange experience of being useful to someone without an angle.
notes: Emmerich=Lion reused from Jost/Emmerich. Kest's sign (the Twins) is her own already-stated sign, reused verbatim. A smaller-scale echo of the Kest/Kheldar rivalry chain, deliberately: same thief, different discrepancy-professional, different resolution (help instead of a working peace). Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Diadem's two mounted couriers -- one horse, one wing -- end up delivering the same dispatch twice, redundantly, and spend the debrief arguing whose route was actually faster instead of who wasted the ride. B: Sigrun clocks that Waldrada takes the long way around certain checkpoints on purpose, and asks why. Waldrada admits some of those checkpoints are staffed by people she used to answer to under the assembly, and she's not ready to be recognized yet. A: Sigrun, whose own worst habit is saying the true thing at the worst possible moment, tells her outright: avoiding the checkpoint doesn't undo the defection, it just makes her look like she's still choosing a side by hiding from one. Waldrada, still weighing the whole question the way she weighs everything, admits Sigrun's right and hates that the shortest path is also the one she has to fly in the open. She starts taking the direct route. Sigrun starts riding escort on that leg, unasked, so being seen doesn't mean being seen alone.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Sigrun=Archer from Ricberta/Sigrun, Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda). Both diadem-route mounted couriers -- Archer's failure mode ('says the true thing at the worst moment') as the literal mechanism that forces Scales' failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') into the open. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Sigrun's dispatches keep arriving at the dole line with bad news -- shortages, delays -- and Maren's started associating her specifically with things getting worse, unfairly, since Sigrun's only ever the messenger. B: Sigrun, stung by being blamed for news she didn't make, tells Maren plainly that shooting the courier doesn't fix the shortage. Maren admits she knows that and does it anyway, because Sigrun's the only part of the bad news she can actually see arrive, and the dole line needs somewhere to put the feeling that isn't the shortage itself. A: Sigrun offers a trade instead of an argument: she'll start bringing Maren the numbers a day early, off the record, so the dole line has more time to plan instead of just react to bad news landing on top of it. Maren, whose whole practice is deciding who gets her real attention, recognizes the offer for what it is -- not an apology, a fix -- and gives Sigrun the thing she actually wants back: being seen as useful instead of as the shape bad news happens to arrive in.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Sigrun=Archer from Ricberta/Sigrun, Maren=Crab from Avatar/Maren). Archer's own function (the scout who comes back with the thing you needed) complicated by Crab's failure mode (loyalty to people that shows as blame when the news is bad) -- resolved practically, not just emotionally. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Sigrun's dispatches keep arriving at Brandt's gate faster than his own watch rotation can process them; he tells her, without much heat, that speed isn't the same as usefulness if nobody's ready to act on the news. B: Sigrun takes the correction harder than he means it -- being fast and right is the whole of her value, and being told it doesn't land clean is the worst thing anyone's said to her about the job. Brandt, who has never once needed to be fast at anything, admits he only meant his own gate crew is slow, not that her riding wasn't good; the fault was never hers. A: Sigrun admits what actually stung: she says the true thing at the worst moment more often than she'd like, and 'your speed doesn't help if we're not ready' landed exactly like every other time that's cost her. Brandt, whose whole competence is being ready for a hit whenever it lands, tells her that's a gate's job, not a courier's -- she rides it in, he holds what she brings, and neither one has to be the whole system alone. It's the first time being fast has felt like half a job instead of the whole one she has to defend by herself.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Sigrun=Archer from Ricberta/Sigrun, Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Archer's failure mode ('says the true thing at the worst moment') as the literal friction, resolved by Bull's virtue ('holds ground nobody else could') reframed as complementary rather than competing roles. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Two couriers, one diadem one assembly, compare routes and speeds the way any two people who do the exact same job for opposite employers inevitably do -- with more edge than either admits to. B: Sigrun's needling ('your birds fly prettier, mine actually get there') lands somewhere real: Solveig's family expects the prophecy to arrive gracefully, not just arrive, and grace has cost her time on more than one run that mattered. Sigrun didn't know that was the standard she was being measured against, and stops needling once she does. A: Solveig admits she envies that Sigrun's speed is just her own -- nobody's waiting on her arrivals to mean anything beyond the message. Sigrun, whose worst habit is saying the true thing at the worst moment, tells her plainly that a courier who's only ever delivering somebody else's prophecy stops being a courier and starts being cargo -- and offers to race her, actually race her, no family, no stakes, just to remind her which one she is.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Sigrun=Archer from Ricberta/Sigrun, Solveig=Vessel from Brandt/Solveig) -- same unit, same sign, not reassigned. Cross-route (diadem Sigrun, assembly Solveig), post-convergence, both couriers by trade -- the professional mirror is the whole hook. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Sigrun's dispatches keep routing past Torvald's assembly post without stopping, since officially there's nothing left there worth delivering to. Torvald doesn't complain about being skipped; he just keeps standing the post anyway, dispatch or no dispatch. B: Sigrun, curious despite herself, starts actually stopping, and asks why he holds a post nobody's sending him orders for. Torvald's answer is the same one he gives everyone: someone has to, and there's no one left to relieve him of deciding that. A: Sigrun admits she's spent her whole career being the one who ranges out and comes back with news that matters, and doesn't know what she'd do at a post where the news stopped coming. Torvald tells her plainly it's not nothing -- the standing is the news, some days; a post held is its own kind of dispatch, delivered to no one, and still worth riding past to confirm. Sigrun starts routing an actual stop past his post from then on, not because headquarters asks her to, but because somebody should still be the one who checks.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Sigrun=Archer from Ricberta/Sigrun, Torvald=Crab from Dietmar/Torvald). Archer's own function (ranges out, returns with news) set against a post that generates none -- Torvald's Crab loyalty read as its own form of unreceived dispatch. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Sigrun, professionally curious about anyone who travels somewhere and comes back with something, asks Rinsa what the descent is actually like to ride, courier to courier. Rinsa points out she doesn't ride anything, she walks it, every time, on foot, in the dark -- there's no fast way down. B: Sigrun admits the comparison was lazy, and asks a better question: does the answer ever change, run to run. Rinsa says no, that's not what changes -- what changes is who's asking, and she's the one thing that stays constant across every question anyone's ever carried down there. A: Sigrun, whose whole worth is in what she brings back and how fast, admits she's never once thought about what it costs to be the medium and not the message -- to matter only as the route, never the news. Rinsa tells her that's exactly right, and exactly fine; being the road is its own kind of necessary, and Sigrun of all people, whose job is also being a road for other people's urgent things, should already know that isn't nothing. Sigrun stops apologizing for asking a lazy question. She starts actually listening to the answer.
notes: Sigrun=Archer reused from Ricberta/Sigrun. Rinsa's own already-stated sign, the Vessel, reused verbatim. Archer's own function (ranges out, returns with news) set against Vessel's failure mode ('belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody') -- two professions built around carrying something for someone else, argued from opposite ends of what that costs. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Tancred, deep in the Pardoner line's early discipline, tells Waldrada plainly that defection is exactly the kind of thing his order exists to forgive. Waldrada, who has spent years weighing the defection rather than confessing it, finds being pre-forgiven for a decision she hasn't finished making almost insulting. B: Tancred admits he offered the absolution because it's the only tool he has, not because he understood what she actually needed; Waldrada, who has never once had anyone ask instead of judge, tells him the weighing itself is the thing, not the verdict at the end of it -- she needs someone to sit in the deliberation with her, not skip to forgiving its outcome. A: Waldrada explains what the years of deliberation actually cost her -- not doubt about the choice, but the particular loneliness of a decision nobody else was willing to take as seriously as she did. Tancred, who measures people by what they build rather than by verdicts handed down on them, stops offering absolution and starts just asking good questions about the actual weighing -- which turns out to be the only thing that ever helped. Neither calls it forgiveness. It's closer to being taken seriously, which for Waldrada was always the harder ask.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda, Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm). Both diadem-route. Scales' failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') met directly by Goat's virtue (measures people by what they build, not by snap verdicts) -- a support about being taken seriously in the weighing, not absolved of its outcome. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Maren, running the dole line during a cold snap, needs Waldrada's flight roster locked in fast; Waldrada, still weighing whether the diadem's logistics are even trustworthy enough to commit her route to, is late with the answer and costs the line an hour. B: Maren doesn't soften the complaint -- an hour is real, on a dole line, in winter -- and Waldrada, expecting judgment, gets something else instead: Maren asks what she's actually weighing, because indecision this costly usually isn't really about the schedule. Waldrada admits it's the same question it always is: which side actually deserves the commitment. A: Maren tells her plainly that the dole line doesn't have the luxury of that question -- she decided a long time ago who she's loyal to and it was never the crown or the assembly, it was the people in front of her, and Waldrada could try deciding the same way instead of weighing institutions against each other forever. Waldrada doesn't resolve the larger question. She does start locking her schedule to Maren's line specifically, loyalty to one person doing the work that loyalty to a whole side never managed.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda, Maren=Crab from Avatar/Maren). Scales' failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') given a real cost by Crab's virtue (loyalty to people, not causes) -- Maren's practical answer to a question Waldrada's been treating as abstract. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: They meet only after the routes converge -- Edda, assembly's own reciter, wants Waldrada's defection for the record, not gossip, history. Waldrada refuses to be anyone's cautionary verse. B: Reconciling the diadem and assembly muster-rolls (the two sides name things differently) forces them into real proximity. Waldrada catches Edda quietly correcting the diadem clerks' errors without taking credit for it, and reads it as a reciter's habit, not pettiness. A: Waldrada explains the resentment was never about doctrine -- the assembly demanded loyalty run one direction only. Edda, whose entire craft is getting the record right, refuses to let Waldrada's defection get smoothed into either faction's flattering version; she writes it exactly as it happened, unflinching about the parts that make the assembly look bad too. It's the first true account anyone's given her back. S (romance): Waldrada stops flinching when someone asks which side she's really on. Edda's answer is on record, precise, and doesn't require her to pick -- the record just states the truth, in both books.
notes: Waldrada=Scales is new, off her own note ('resentful Assembly flier; loyalty subplot') read as backstory affiliation, not current playable route -- her units.route field is diadem, so she is a defector FROM the assembly, which resolves the apparent contradiction rather than being a data error. The Scales' own failure mode ('delay disguised as deliberation') is the shape of a years-long refusal to say outright which side she actually serves.
