This chain only makes sense post-convergence: chapter numbering jumps from d10/a10 to shared b/c/k/m-prefixed chapters starting around ch_b15, and Waldrada joins diadem (ch_d02) while Edda joins assembly (ch_a02) -- flagged so a future writer doesn't place this scene inside either Act 1 branch.

summary: C: Dietmar, revolution-generation to his core, has opinions about defectors; Waldrada, freshly defected from the assembly, has heard every one of them already and isn't interested in his verdict. B: Dietmar admits the opinions are really about himself -- he's spent so long being the diadem's proof that the old loyalties held that a defector reads to him like an accusation. Waldrada, who's spent the same stretch of time unable to say outright which side she serves, recognizes someone else performing a loyalty he isn't sure he still feels. A: Waldrada tells him plainly that deliberation isn't the same as disloyalty -- she took years weighing it and the assembly earned every year of doubt. Dietmar, who has never once let himself weigh it, admits her question is the one he's been outrunning since the gate-holding deed started feeling more like a museum piece than a duty. Neither talks the other out of anything; they just stop being each other's evidence for a verdict neither one wanted to reach alone.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Waldrada=Scales from Waldrada/Edda, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald above). Both diadem-route (ch_d01/ch_d02) -- a defector and the veteran who's built his whole identity on never having been one. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Tancred asks Maren for a blessing over the dole line, formally, Pardoner-style; Maren tells him blessings don't move grain and she doesn't have time for the ones that don't. B: Tancred, stung, points out he's offering the one thing his class actually has to give; Maren admits she wasn't dismissing the offer, she's just run out of patience for anything that doesn't visibly help, faith included -- and asks him, if he wants to help, to carry crates instead. A: Tancred carries crates, for weeks, without complaint, and Maren admits she underestimated what a Pardoner's discipline actually looks like in practice -- unglamorous, repeated, not asking for credit. Tancred tells her the crates were never separate from the blessing, just the part of it that shows; Maren, who measures loyalty in exactly that kind of showing up, gives him something rarer than absolution: she trusts him with the line unsupervised.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm, Maren=Crab from Avatar/Maren). Goat's virtue ('will do the unglamorous work for years') proven rather than argued -- Maren's own Crab failure mode (loyalty that shows in action, not words) sets the terms of what actually earns her trust. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Tancred, working through the Pardoner line's early absolutions, offers Solveig one for whatever she thinks she's guilty of regarding the family prophecy. Solveig tells him there's nothing to absolve -- she didn't do anything, it was just handed to her, which is somehow worse. B: Tancred admits he doesn't actually have a rite for that -- his whole class handles sin, choices made and needing forgiving, not inheritance nobody chose. Solveig, hearing her situation correctly named as outside his order's whole framework for the first time, feels less alone in it rather than more, just from being accurately placed instead of misfiled as guilt. A: Solveig admits what she actually needs isn't forgiveness, it's someone to witness that the prophecy was never a choice and still cost her one anyway. Tancred, who measures people by what they build rather than what's been built onto them, tells her plainly: nothing she's inherited counts against what she chooses to build from here, and he'll hold her to that measure instead of the family's. Solveig doesn't stop carrying the prophecy. She starts building something of her own alongside it, with someone keeping the second, honest score.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm, Solveig=Vessel from Brandt/Solveig). Cross-route (diadem/assembly), post-convergence. Goat's virtue (measures people by what they build) offered as an alternative to Vessel's failure mode ('belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody') -- a support about being measured by choice rather than inheritance. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Anselm can't finish a blessing without a caveat attached, and Tancred, still new enough to the Pardoner line to want them uncomplicated, finds this maddening in a way he can't fully justify. B: Tancred admits the caveats are the only part of Anselm's theology he's started to trust -- a monk who insists on his own uncertainty is at least not lying to him, unlike the men Tancred grew up under. Anselm, for the first time, says something without immediately qualifying it. A: Anselm confesses the dissolved boundary cuts both ways -- he understands why the people he's meant to condemn do what they do, and can no longer do the condemning cleanly, which reads as failure by every measure the order taught him. Tancred, who measures people by what they've built, refuses to measure Anselm by what he's stopped being able to do. S (romance): neither one resolves the other's problem, and it turns out that was never the ask. Tancred's climb gets a companion who won't let him mistake the climbing for the point; Anselm's dissolved certainties get one fixed thing he doesn't have to argue himself out of.
notes: Both signs new, off each unit's own note. Tancred=Goat ('village recruit; Pardoner line' -- climbs, unglamorous work for years, measures people by what they've built -- a penitential class line built from humble origins is exactly that climb). Anselm=Fishes ('adrift monk; theology barometer' -- dissolves the boundary, understands the enemy too well to hate or fight them -- a monk whose faith has come unmoored into total ambivalence is the Fishes' failure mode as a starting condition, not an endpoint). Goat's own failure mode (measures people by output) is the exact friction the A-support resolves by Tancred explicitly refusing to apply it.

summary: C: Tancred, still new enough to the Pardoner line to take it seriously, tries to extract a confession out of Kheldar for the manifest fraud everyone quietly knows about. Kheldar finds the attempt almost sweet and declines to be absolved of a sin he doesn't consider one. B: Tancred presses on principle, not results -- he says the confession was never really for Kheldar's sake, it's for his own, practicing the unglamorous work of holding someone to account even when it changes nothing. Kheldar, unused to being pursued without an angle, starts actually answering the questions instead of deflecting them, if only out of professional curiosity about a man who wants nothing from him. A: Kheldar admits, obliquely, that he keeps a private ledger of the debts he actually can't repay -- not the profitable discrepancies, the other kind -- and has never shown it to anyone. Tancred doesn't ask to see it; he tells Kheldar that's closer to penance than anything Tancred's own line teaches, since nobody assigned it to him and nobody's grading it. Kheldar doesn't confess to anything. He does, for the first time, let someone watch him not lie about not confessing.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Tancred=Goat from Tancred/Anselm, Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest). Direct moral-code friction: Tancred's own note ('village recruit; Pardoner line') is explicitly a forgiveness/penance class line, set against Kheldar's own note ('manifest discrepancy thread') -- a penitent and an unrepentant profiteer, deliberately not resolved into either converting the other. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Brandt's shield arm takes a hit that should have ended his rotation for the week; Maren, running the dole line short-handed, patches him fast and rough and tells him to sit down before she makes it an order. He doesn't sit down. She notices he doesn't, and files it. B: Maren starts treating Brandt's gate post as a second stop on her rounds, not because he asks, but because he's the one soldier on the wall who'll actually report an injury before it's an emergency -- which she reads correctly as him trusting her enough not to make him look weak for it. A: Brandt admits the gate holds because he's decided it has to, not because he's actually as sturdy as the post -- and that Maren's the only one who's caught the gap between those two things without using it against him. Maren, who's spent her whole practice deciding which people get her real attention instead of her rationed attention, makes her decision plain: she starts teaching him the forms that turn a shield-sergeant into someone who can actually take the hits he's been absorbing on will alone. The Great Shield he earns after isn't hers to take credit for. It's the first time either of them built something instead of just enduring it.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Maren=Crab from Avatar/Maren, Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig). This is the class-unlock chain already referenced in units.u_brandt's own note ('Great shield via Maren support'), finally written -- kept platonic/mentorship, not romantic, consistent with the earlier decision (see the Brandt/Solveig and Ricberta/Brandt chains) to keep Brandt's canon class-unlock ally distinct from his actual romance-flagged option. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Two faith-tree healers argue their first triage call opposite ways -- Anselm wants to bless the dying properly even if it costs the line time; Maren wants the line moving, blessing be damned, because more people live that way. B: Anselm admits he can't finish a blessing without a caveat lately, doctrine gone loose in his hands, and watching Maren work without any of his doubt looks like a mercy he's lost the knack for. Maren corrects him: it's not certainty, it's that she decided a long time ago which people she's loyal to, and the dole line always wins the tiebreak. A: Maren admits the certainty is a mask over the same doubt his caveats are honest about -- she's just better at not showing it while the line's still moving. Anselm, whose whole practice has become sitting in the doubt rather than hiding it, offers her the one thing his theology's actually good for: permission to not have it worked out yet and keep working anyway. It's the first time anyone's told her the mask doesn't have to be a wound.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Maren=Crab from Avatar/Maren, Anselm=Fishes from Tancred/Anselm). Both faith-tree healers (cls_tr_faith), assembly-route, direct doctrine-vs-practice friction. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Maren's dole allotments keep coming up short in ways that trace, eventually, back to Kheldar's manifest games; she corners him expecting to have to threaten someone for once. B: Kheldar, who has never once been cornered by someone who wasn't after a cut, is thrown by a healer who just wants the shortage to stop, no leverage implied. He offers, half as a joke, to make her specific shortage disappear -- meaning fixed, not hidden. A: Maren takes the offer and makes her terms plain: she doesn't care what else he moves through his manifests, only that her line stays whole, and she'll know if it doesn't. Kheldar, who has spent his whole career being the discrepancy nobody can pin down, finds himself pinned down anyway, by someone with no leverage over him at all except that he'd have to look at himself if her line went hungry on his account. He keeps the deal. He doesn't examine too closely why hers is the one account he balances for free.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Maren=Crab from Avatar/Maren, Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest). Crab's virtue (loyal past reason, to people not causes) as the one thing in Kheldar's orbit he can't out-negotiate, since she isn't negotiating. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Solveig's courier runs land her at Brandt's gate on a fixed schedule. He starts timing his own rounds to be the one who opens it, which he tells himself is just efficient gatekeeping. B: Solveig admits the schedule isn't fixed at all -- she reroutes to make Brandt's gate the last stop, because it's the only post on her circuit where nobody expects her to already know how things turn out. Brandt, who has held the same gate for years without needing to be more than reliable, doesn't know what to do with being someone's exception. A: Solveig explains the family holds her prophecy in trust the way a garrison holds a gate -- not hers to decide, only to carry until it's needed -- and that no one has ever once asked what she wants instead. Brandt, who measures his own worth in whether the gate held, tells her the gate was never the whole job; someone still has to decide, every day, that it's worth holding. It's the first time being wanted for something other than the outcome has been put to her plainly. S (romance): Solveig starts flying the long way around just to land somewhere nobody's waiting on a prophecy from; Brandt gets a reason to be more than the gate that held -- someone on the other side of it who chooses to keep coming back.
notes: Brandt=Bull is new, off his own note ('gate sergeant', cls_tr_lance/gp_armor) -- a defensive tank who literally holds a gate, the most literal possible read of the Bull's 'will not be moved,' chosen deliberately over a more oblique match. Solveig=Vessel is new, off her own note ('highland pegasus courier; living-prophecy family' -- inherited into a role she didn't choose and carries for others, the Vessel's failure mode 'belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody' read as family inheritance rather than Rinsa's professional/oracular version of the same sign). Brandt's existing 'Great shield via Maren support' note (units.u_brandt) is a separate class-unlock chain, preserved as-is and not folded into this pairing -- this is Brandt's distinct, actually-romance-flagged option, per the original skeleton note.

summary: C: Brandt holds the gate; Gunnar covers it from the wall above with a crossbow, and after the first real assault they compare notes on whose position actually mattered more. Neither backs down. B: Gunnar admits, grudgingly, that his aim's only as good as the time the gate buys him to line up a shot -- Brandt's stubbornness isn't just holding ground, it's manufacturing the seconds Gunnar's whole craft depends on. Brandt, who's spent his career being underestimated as simple muscle, hadn't considered that the gate was ever anyone's clock. A: Brandt admits he measures his own worth purely in whether the gate held, nothing more complicated than that; Gunnar, decades further into the same kind of unglamorous, solitary discipline, tells him that's the wrong measure for either of them -- the gate holding is what the standard produces, not what it is. Two men who each assumed they were the whole defense find out, plainly, neither one of them was ever meant to be.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig, Gunnar=Goat from Gunnar/Edda). Both assembly-route. Bull's virtue ('holds ground nobody else could') and Goat's virtue ('will do the unglamorous work for years') read as literally complementary combat roles (gate + overwatch) before becoming a philosophical point about measuring one's own worth. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Brandt, gate sergeant, and Torvald, last of a dead order, hold adjacent posts on the same wall; Brandt asks him once why he never requests relief, and Torvald asks him right back why he'd ever want it. B: Brandt admits he's never actually wanted relief either -- he just assumed everyone did, and asking felt like the polite thing rather than the honest one. Torvald tells him there's no politeness left in his own case, just the plain fact that holding the post is the only shape his loyalty has left to take, and he'd rather take that shape than none. A: Brandt admits his own gate isn't so different -- he measures his whole worth in whether it holds, same as Torvald measures his in showing up for an order that can't order him anymore. Torvald tells him that's not nothing, and it's not the same as his own case either: Brandt's gate still has a Baron behind it who'd notice if it fell; Torvald's post doesn't, and he holds it anyway. Two men who both mistook holding for the whole job find, side by side on the same wall, that the mistake was smaller than they thought -- the post was never the whole job, but it also was never nothing.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Brandt=Bull from Brandt/Solveig, Torvald=Crab from Dietmar/Torvald). Both assembly-route. Bull's virtue ('holds ground nobody else could') set beside Crab's virtue (loyal past reason) as two adjacent, structurally similar postures on the same wall, differentiated by what's still watching. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Edda wants the family prophecy recited to her exactly as Solveig's house tells it, word for word, for the record. Solveig gives her the official version, flawless, rehearsed -- the one she's recited a hundred times for people who wanted exactly that. B: Edda, whose whole craft is catching discrepancies, notices the recitation's too flawless, too rehearsed, and asks what the unofficial version sounds like. Solveig admits there isn't one, not because it doesn't exist, but because she's never been asked for it before -- only ever the official one, by everyone, always. A: Solveig gives her the real version, halting, unrehearsed, full of the parts the family edits out -- what it actually felt like to be handed a destiny before she could talk. Edda writes it down exactly as given and tells her that's the first honest account of a prophecy she's ever gotten, since every other one she's recorded came pre-smoothed by whoever was reciting it. Solveig doesn't stop performing the official version when it's asked for. She does, for the first time, have an unofficial one on record somewhere that isn't just hers to carry alone.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Solveig=Vessel from Brandt/Solveig, Edda=Maiden from Waldrada/Edda). Maiden's virtue ('notices the discrepancy nobody else did') applied directly to Vessel's failure mode ('belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody') -- catching that even Solveig's own account of herself has been edited for an audience. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Solveig, curious what an actual oracle does with prophecy once it's spoken, asks Rinsa what happens to the answers people carry back up. Rinsa's answer -- she doesn't keep track, it was never hers to keep -- unsettles Solveig more than a mystical one would have. B: Rinsa notices Solveig flinch at the word 'carry' and asks what she's carrying that isn't a question. Solveig admits her whole family's prophecy was never asked, either -- it was handed to her already answered, and she's spent her life being the vessel for a message she didn't get to receive fresh. A: Rinsa, who pours herself out professionally and has never once needed the customer's question to matter to her personally, tells Solveig the difference that's been eating her without a name: Rinsa chose the emptying, every time, at the door, and can walk back out of it; Solveig was filled before she could choose anything. Solveig, hearing her own condition named by someone who does it on purpose and still keeps a self underneath, asks the only useful question left: how. Rinsa doesn't have a clean answer. She offers to find out with her, which is the first time either Vessel's been asked to keep something instead of pouring it out.
notes: Both units already carry the Vessel sign from their own established chains (Solveig from Brandt/Solveig, Rinsa from her own units row / Rinsa/Kest) -- deliberately paired as a mirror rather than avoided: two Vessels, argued as genuinely distinct (Solveig's family-inherited emptying vs Rinsa's chosen, professional one), with the mirroring itself as the chain's actual subject rather than a coincidence to write around. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Edda's recitations keep getting Gunnar's own hunting stories wrong in small, specific ways. He corrects her once, gruffly, expecting that to be the end of it. B: Edda keeps coming back for more corrections -- not because the poem needs to be accurate, but because she's cataloguing which details he insists on, and they turn out to be the parts he actually cares about, not the ones that make the best verse. A: Gunnar admits he doesn't care whether the recitation is accurate for its own sake; he cares that someone still bothers to ask a huntsman his age which parts of his life were real. Edda, whose whole craft is preserving things exactly as they were before they're gone, tells him the corrections were never charity -- the record is better for them, and so is she. S (romance): Gunnar stops treating her questions as an old man being humored; Edda gets a source who argues with her draft instead of accepting whatever she writes -- the collaboration neither expected to need turns out to be the one that lasts.
notes: Gunnar=Goat is new, off his own note ('old huntsman; crossbow-certified' -- decades of solitary, unglamorous, exacting work, the Goat's own virtue read as sustained craft rather than Tancred's institutional-climb version of the same sign). Edda=Maiden reused from the Waldrada/Edda chain above -- same unit, same sign, not reassigned.

summary: C: Anselm, doctrine gone loose with doubt, asks Gunnar how a huntsman squares killing game with whatever faith he keeps. Gunnar's answer is short: he doesn't keep one, and the game doesn't need him to. B: Anselm presses -- surely decades of it wears a mark on a man -- and Gunnar admits it does, just not a doctrinal one; he's just gotten exact about which kills are necessary and which aren't, and stopped needing a theology to tell him the difference. Anselm, whose whole crisis is that doctrine's stopped telling him the difference either, hears something like an answer he wasn't expecting from a huntsman. A: Gunnar tells him plainly that forty years of exactness is its own kind of faith, whatever you call it, and Anselm's caveats might be the same thing arriving from the other direction -- not a faith collapsing, a faith getting exact. Anselm, who's spent the whole crisis assuming the doubt was failure, takes the reframe seriously for the first time: not a theology dissolving, a theology narrowing down to what actually holds. Neither converts the other. Gunnar gets a monk who stops asking him for absolution he never needed; Anselm gets a model for what exactness looks like without a doctrine attached.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Gunnar=Goat from Gunnar/Edda, Anselm=Fishes from Tancred/Anselm). Goat's virtue (sustained, exacting, unglamorous craft) offered as an alternate model to Fishes' failure mode ('understands the enemy too well to fight them') -- exactness without doctrine as an answer to doctrine dissolving into ambivalence. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Gunnar, sharpening a bolt as usual, tells Dietmar plainly he's never heard of him -- the revolution, the legend, none of it reached an assembly huntsman's ears out on the old border. Dietmar, used to being recognized everywhere in diadem circles, finds the anonymity almost refreshing and almost insulting in equal measure. B: Dietmar admits, once the insult wears off, that being unrecognized here is the first honest read he's gotten on whether the legend still holds up without the legend attached -- and it mostly does, which surprises him. Gunnar, who has spent his whole career being competent without being known for it, tells him that's just what the work is like for most people; Dietmar's the unusual one, not Gunnar. A: Gunnar admits he's never once needed anyone to know what he can do, only that it gets done, and asks Dietmar honestly whether the being-seen part was ever actually about the revolution or just something he picked up along the way and never put down. Dietmar doesn't have a clean answer, but for the first time he says he doesn't need one -- a huntsman nobody's heard of just did him the favor of being competent, unbothered, and entirely unimpressed, and it's the most useful he's felt in the whole obsolescence arc.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Gunnar=Goat from Gunnar/Edda, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald). Cross-route (assembly/diadem). Goat's virtue (unglamorous work, no audience required) as the direct counter-example to Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully') -- competence that never needed witnessing in the first place. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: The assembly's two oldest hands size each other up across a training yard -- a huntsman who's outlasted three commanding officers and a knight who's outlasted his entire order. B: Gunnar, sharpening a crossbow bolt with more attention than it needs, asks Torvald outright how he keeps showing up to guard people for an order that isn't there to order him to. Torvald's answer is short: someone has to, and he's the only one left who remembers how. A: Gunnar admits he's not sure his own decades of solitary, exacting work have added up to anything an army needs, just a very good aim and no one left to impress with it. Torvald tells him that's the wrong measure -- an order dies, the standard it kept doesn't have to, and Gunnar's kept his own standard for longer without anyone watching than Torvald's own men managed with a whole chapel behind them. Two old men who assumed nobody was still counting find out they've both been counted.
notes: Gunnar=Goat reused from Gunnar/Edda. Torvald=Crab reused from Dietmar/Torvald above -- same unit, same sign. Both assembly-route, both the roster's oldest recruitable veterans outside the jagen pair itself. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Gunnar, curious about a profession stranger than his own, asks Rinsa how she tracks a customer's nerve on the way down -- what she's watching for. Rinsa's answer sounds uncannily like his own hunting method: not the person, the pattern; not this trip, the hundreds before it. B: Rinsa admits the comparison's apt -- both of them do the same unglamorous, exacting thing for decades, alone, and get good at it precisely because nobody's there to perform for. Gunnar, whose whole craft has never once needed an audience, recognizes a kindred discipline in a job that looks nothing like his own from the outside. A: Gunnar admits the part nobody asks him about is what forty years of that solitary exactness costs -- not the skill, the isolation the skill requires. Rinsa, who pours herself out for strangers professionally and has never had the cost of it named back to her by someone doing the same trade from a different direction, tells him plainly: it costs exactly what he thinks, and it's still worth doing right. Two people who do the same private, exacting work in completely different fields end up being the only ones who actually understand what the other one does all day.
notes: Gunnar=Goat reused from Gunnar/Edda. Rinsa's own already-stated sign, the Vessel, reused verbatim. Goat's virtue (unglamorous, solitary, exacting craft) recognized directly in Vessel's own professional practice (the descent, done hundreds of times, for strangers) -- two very different jobs built on the same discipline. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Gunnar catches Kest casing the assembly armory with the flat, professional patience of someone who's tracked plenty of things smarter than a startled deer. He doesn't report her. He tells her she's good, but not as good as she thinks, and offers to prove it. B: Kest, insulted and curious in equal measure, takes him up on it -- a stalking contest, her against his decades of reading a treeline. She loses, badly, and can't figure out how he read her approach before she'd committed to it. A: Gunnar tells her the trick isn't the tracking, it's refusing to move until the argument in his own head about the best approach has actually settled -- something he's had forty years to get right and she's still doing live, mid-job, which is why she hesitates at the worst moments. Kest admits that's exactly her problem, and exactly why she's never been caught taking something she meant to walk away from and never quite has. Gunnar doesn't offer to fix it. He offers to keep hunting with her until the two voices in her head learn his patience instead of each other's noise.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Gunnar=Goat from Gunnar/Edda, Kest=Twins her own already-stated sign). A hunter's patient single-mindedness set against a thief's arguing-both-sides indecision -- Goat's virtue (sustained, exacting craft) as the literal fix for the Twins' failure mode (won't commit while a better argument exists). Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Edda wants Anselm's blessings recited word for word, every caveat included, for the record; Anselm finds this faintly absurd -- nobody preserves the hedge, they preserve the promise. B: Edda insists the hedge is the actual content -- a monk's caveats are the only honest theology on record anywhere in her collection, and she's not going to be the one who edits him into false certainty for posterity. Anselm, who's spent the whole crisis assuming his doubt makes him a worse record than a confident man, hears his own uncertainty called valuable for the first time. A: Anselm admits he's been quietly grateful someone's writing the doubt down at all, since it means it existed, whatever happens to his faith after. Edda tells him plainly: the record doesn't care if he resolves it, only that it's true when it's written -- and his caveats are more true than most of what she's had to preserve from men who never doubted anything in their lives. Anselm stops apologizing for the hedges. Edda gets the most honestly-transcribed theology in her whole collection.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Edda=Maiden from Waldrada/Edda, Anselm=Fishes from Tancred/Anselm). Both assembly-route. Direct tie: Edda's own note ('village reciter') as the record-keeper who values Anselm's own note ('theology barometer') -- his doubt-riddled caveats -- as the truest theology in her whole collection, rather than something to be edited into false confidence. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Edda wants Kheldar's story for the record -- smuggler-spy, unkillable, escapes everything -- and he politely declines to be recorded at all, on the professional grounds that a documented man is a traceable one. B: Edda points out she already has half his story from everyone else's accounts of him, badly, secondhand, and getting it wrong; if he won't correct the record, the record stays wrong, which she finds more insulting on his behalf than he seems to. Kheldar, who has never once cared what anyone thinks they know about him, is oddly needled by the idea of a bad, inaccurate account of himself outliving the accurate one nobody has. A: Kheldar strikes a deal, characteristically: he'll correct exactly the parts that are wrong, on the record, on the condition she never writes down where he actually is at the time of telling. Edda agrees, and gets the strangest, most carefully redacted true account in her whole collection -- accurate about everything except the one thing that would matter to anyone trying to catch him. It's the closest thing to being honestly known that Kheldar's ever allowed anyone.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Edda=Maiden from Waldrada/Edda, Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest). Direct tie: Edda's own note ('village reciter,' keeper of the record) applied to Kheldar's own note ('manifest discrepancy thread,' a man who exists to not be pinned down) -- the negotiation over what gets recorded is the whole chain. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Edda wants Dietmar's account of the revolution for the record, the real one, not the version already circulating as legend. Dietmar gives her the legend anyway, out of old habit, and she calls him on the substitution immediately. B: Dietmar admits the legend is easier to tell because the real account doesn't have a shape yet that ends well -- he's still in it, still trying to be useful, and a record only really works once the story's finished. Edda tells him plainly that's not how any record she's ever kept actually works; half of them are unfinished, and the unfinished ones are usually the most honest. A: Dietmar gives her the real account -- not the revolution's, just his own, obsolescence and all, admitting he doesn't know yet whether the gate-holding deed will read as a last good chapter or a footnote nobody needed. Edda writes it down exactly as given, unfinished, and tells him that's precisely what makes it worth keeping: a legend already knows how it ends, a true record doesn't, and his is still being written whether he likes it or not.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Edda=Maiden from Waldrada/Edda, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald). Lion's failure mode ('cannot take a demotion gracefully') read as a preference for legend over an unfinished, unflattering true account; Maiden's virtue ('notices the discrepancy nobody else did') is the literal mechanism that catches him substituting one for the other. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Edda wants to record what the oracle actually says, verbatim, for the archive; Rinsa tells her that's not how it works -- the oracle doesn't say anything to her, only to the person who descended, and she's just the one who leads them down and back. B: Edda, undeterred, asks to record Rinsa's part instead -- the leading, the waiting, the hundreds of times. Rinsa finds this stranger than being asked for the oracle's words; nobody's ever wanted the guide's account before, only the destination's. A: Rinsa gives it to her, plainly, without performance -- what the stairs feel like on the two-hundredth trip, how she tells if someone's about to lose their nerve, what she does with her own thoughts while she waits in the dark for a stranger's question to finish. Edda writes all of it down and tells her it's the first account in her whole collection of someone who does the actual carrying instead of just receiving what gets carried. Rinsa, who pours herself out for a living and has never once had any of it kept, finds out what it's like to have some of it kept anyway.
notes: Edda=Maiden reused from Waldrada/Edda. Rinsa's own already-stated sign, the Vessel, reused verbatim. Direct tie: Edda's own note ('village reciter,' the record-keeper) turned toward Rinsa's own note (the one unit who's actually descended) -- the first time anyone in the archive records the guide instead of the destination. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Anselm, theology gone loose with doubt, wants to know what Rinsa actually saw down at the Throat -- not the oracle's answer, the descent itself. Rinsa, who's led hundreds of people down and up, finds the question almost quaint; everyone wants the answer, no one's ever asked about the stairs. B: Rinsa admits the stairs are the only honest part of the job -- the answer's whatever the customer needed to hear, but the dark is the same dark for everyone who goes down it. Anselm, whose whole crisis is that he understands too many sides of a question to condemn any of them cleanly, recognizes in her an authority that doesn't come from doctrine at all, just from having actually been there. A: Rinsa admits she's never told anyone what she believes is actually down there, because belief was never required for the job -- she pours out whatever the descent needs of her and keeps nothing back for herself, including her own certainty. Anselm offers the one thing his dissolved theology still has: he doesn't need her to believe anything to trust what she saw. It's the first support of her life where being asked wasn't also being asked to perform an answer.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim from their own established chains (Anselm=Fishes from Tancred/Anselm, Rinsa=Vessel from her own units row / the Rinsa/Kest chain). Direct thematic tie: Rinsa's own note calls her 'the only unit who has BEEN down there' regarding the Venerated's death, and Anselm's own note calls him a 'theology barometer' -- this chain is the one place a doctrinal crisis meets someone whose authority comes from experience, not doctrine, before the Act 3 question about the Venerated is ever asked. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Dietmar, who fought for the diadem's legitimacy before Kheldar was old enough to profit off it, wants to know how a man who serves no side at all sleeps at night. Kheldar's answer -- very well, thank you -- is not the confrontation Dietmar came for. B: Dietmar presses harder than the question deserves, and Kheldar, reading the real target, points out that a revolution fought for legitimacy and a smuggling trade fought for margin have the same actual output: both of them decide who gets to eat this winter, one of them just admits the profit motive out loud. Dietmar doesn't have a clean rebuttal. A: Dietmar admits what's actually eating him -- the revolution he bled for produced exactly the kind of grey, transactional peace Kheldar profits off of, and some nights that looks less like victory than like the thing they fought to prevent, just slower. Kheldar, who has made an entire life out of refusing to be anyone's evidence for a verdict, tells him the honest thing: the peace holding at all, ugly and profitable and unglamorous, is probably the only kind that was ever actually available to hold. Dietmar doesn't forgive him for being right. He does stop needling him about it, which from Dietmar is the same thing.
notes: Both signs reused verbatim (Kheldar=Scorpion from Kheldar/Kest, Dietmar=Lion from Dietmar/Torvald). Direct ideological friction: Dietmar's own note ('revolution-generation; obsolescence arc') as an idealist confronting the transactional peace Kheldar's own note ('manifest discrepancy thread') literally profits from -- neither convinces the other, which is the point. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Kest recognizes Kheldar's manifest discrepancies for exactly what they are, because she's been running the same trick smaller and poorer her whole life; she corners him wanting either a cut or an explanation. B: Kheldar offers neither -- offers instead an assessment: she's good enough to be dangerous to him specifically, and he'd rather know where she is than have her loose in his ledgers. Kest hears this as respect dressed as threat, which is closer to true than either of them says out loud. A: Kest admits she never takes more than what an economy this shrunken has already lost; Kheldar, whose whole trade runs on discrepancies nobody's tracking closely enough to miss, recognizes the same code he doesn't follow himself and doesn't insult her by pretending otherwise. What they land on isn't trust, it's the working peace two professionals reach when neither one's stupid enough to make the other an enemy over scraps -- and Kheldar, for the first time on record, tells someone a true number.
notes: Kest's sign (the Twins) is her own already-stated sign, reused verbatim. Kheldar=Scorpion is new, off his own note ('smuggler merchant-spy... manifest discrepancy thread' -- an information broker who trades in what he remembers and what he can hold over someone, the Scorpion's virtue 'carries the grudge that keeps everyone honest' read as leverage rather than personal grievance). Rivalry-to-working-peace chain between Nikaia's two underworld professionals; capped at A, no romance flag (deliberately platonic -- two people whose whole skillset is not attaching to anything).

summary: C: Two old soldiers from opposite prologues, thrown together once the routes converge, sizing each other up as artifacts of a war nobody under thirty remembers. Dietmar wants to know if Torvald's order died well; Torvald wants to know why Dietmar's still trying to be someone's last good memory of the revolution. B: Dietmar admits the obsolescence stings worse than any wound -- being kept around as a symbol, not a soldier. Torvald's answer isn't sympathy, it's correction: his whole order is dead and he's still here holding a post for people who aren't; Dietmar, by comparison, still has a war to be useful in, he's just too proud to notice. A: Dietmar takes the correction the way only another veteran could land it, and starts fighting for the gate-holding deed the way Torvald's been holding his post all along -- not for the record, because there's a body of men behind him worth it. Torvald, watching Dietmar finally stop performing the revolution and start doing the actual unglamorous work of it, extends the closest thing he has left to give: he calls him brother-in-arms, and means the second word literally, for the first time since the plague took his own.
notes: Dietmar=Lion is new, off his own note ('revolution-generation; obsolescence arc' -- an old-guard hero whose identity depends on being seen as one, now fading, the Lion's failure mode 'cannot take a demotion gracefully' as the literal obsolescence arc). Torvald=Crab is new, off his own note ('last of a plague-gutted order; force-deployed' -- loyal past reason to an order that no longer exists to give orders, the Crab's virtue/failure pair exactly) -- a third distinct Crab (after Ricberta's military-secrecy and Maren's medical-scarcity readings), argued here as institutional loyalty that survives its own institution's death; the repetition is deliberate, not a shortcut, per the signs tab's own allowance for 18 units over 12 signs. Both jagens, cross-route (diadem/assembly), so this only makes sense post-convergence, same convention as Waldrada/Edda. Platonic chain, capped at A (no S) -- non-romantic chains in this pass cap at A, reserving S for the 10 romance-flagged chains.

summary: C: Torvald catches Kest lifting a coin off a dead man's belt during a battlefield sweep and says nothing about the theft, only that the dead don't need it argued over. Kest, mid-argument with herself as usual, is unsettled that he clocked the argument and not the theft. B: Kest needles him about outliving an entire order -- doesn't he argue with himself about why he's the one left. Torvald says no, flatly; the arguing stopped being useful a long time ago, it's just grief now, and grief doesn't need two sides. Kest goes quiet in a way that isn't her usual quiet. A: Kest admits, closer to the truth than she's told anyone, that her own arguing used to be a real second voice and isn't anymore, and she doesn't know if losing the argument or losing the reason for it hurt worse. Torvald, who has exactly one answer to that question and has had years to sit with it, tells her it's both, always both, and that the day it stops being both is the day to worry. It's the closest anyone in the roster comes to naming what's actually wrong with her, without either of them saying her brother's name.
notes: Torvald=Crab reused from Ricberta/Torvald above. Kest's sign (the Twins) is her own already-stated sign, reused verbatim. Direct thematic tie to Kest's own note (grieving a twin brother, hidden until supports 'earn the reveal') and Torvald's own note (sole survivor of a wiped order) -- both carry an unspoken grief the chain gestures at without cashing in the full reveal, consistent with her own note that the reveal is meant to surface gradually across her support web, not in any single chain. Platonic chain, capped at A.

summary: C: Kest cases the oracle's approach out of habit, not intent, and gets caught doing it by the one person working there who isn't clergy and doesn't care. Rinsa's take: everyone the descender meets is already asking her for something; a thief casing the place for a change is almost restful. B: Kest can't settle on whether Rinsa's refusal to say if the oracle is real is honesty or the longest con in Nikaia, and says so, expecting an argument. Rinsa agrees it could be either, offers no tiebreak, and goes back to work -- which unsettles Kest more than a denial would have. A: Rinsa points out, flatly, that Kest never actually takes anything from her -- no mark, no angle, just circling. Kest's answer is the closest thing to a confession she gives anyone: she doesn't know how to want something without a plan for losing it cleanly, and Rinsa is not a clean loss. S (romance): two people built to give nothing of themselves away for keeps find the one exception is each other -- Kest stops arguing herself out of it, Rinsa stops pouring herself into strangers long enough to keep something back on purpose, for once, for someone in particular.
notes: Rinsa's sign (the Vessel) is already stated on her own units row, reused verbatim, not reassigned. Kest=Twins is new, off her own note ('prodigious thief... picking through the ruin of an economy rather than preying on' -- implies a thief who constantly argues the moral case for her own targets, the Twins' own virtue/failure -- sees the case against her own position, won't commit while a better argument exists -- matches a Locke-Lamora-archetype code-bound thief exactly). Twins-won't-commit x Vessel-belongs-to-nobody is two different roads to the same non-attachment, which the S-support is built to break, not resolve away.
